title: Fasting before tests, procedures and medicines: getting the instructions right
intro: Medical fasting means avoiding specified food or drink for a defined period before a test, treatment or medicine. It is not the same as choosing a diet. Requirements vary: not every blood test, scan or local-anesthetic procedure requires fasting. The instructions from the service performing your procedure take priority over general advice or another person’s experience.

sections.heading: Ask why fasting is needed and for exact times
paragraphs: Food can affect some blood measurements or prevent a clear view during an examination. With some anesthesia or sedation, stomach contents could enter the lungs if protective reflexes are reduced. Ask whether fasting is actually necessary, when to stop each type of food and drink, and whether the time relates to arrival or the procedure itself. Request written instructions in a language you understand. Do not make the fast longer just to be extra careful; unnecessary restriction can cause discomfort, dehydration or medication problems.

sections.heading: Clarify what counts as food and permitted fluid
paragraphs: Solid food, milk, formula, breast milk and clear liquids are not interchangeable and may have different cutoffs. A drink that looks light is not automatically a permitted clear fluid; milk in coffee and juice with pulp can matter. Ask specifically about water, chewing gum, sweets, smoking and any special preparation drinks. Children’s instructions may differ from adults’. Bowel preparation is a separate process with its own rules. Follow your department’s exact plan rather than applying a universal interval found online.

sections.heading: Get a separate plan for every regular medicine
paragraphs: Tell the team all prescribed and non-prescription medicines, injections, supplements and herbal products. Ask which to take, delay or adjust, whether a small amount of water is allowed, and when to restart. Diabetes treatments, blood thinners and medicines that affect stomach emptying need particular discussion. Do not stop essential medicines or choose a different dose yourself. Taking a medicine on an empty stomach follows that medicine’s own instructions; it does not automatically mean skipping a whole meal or copying a surgical fast.

sections.heading: Plan ahead if fasting could put you at risk
paragraphs: Tell the service about diabetes, pregnancy, frailty, kidney problems, swallowing difficulties or previous problems with fasting. Arrange an individual glucose-monitoring and treatment plan if relevant. Do not ignore symptoms of low blood sugar in order to protect an appointment: follow your agreed emergency plan and seek help, then tell the procedure team. Ask about support for children or anyone unable to understand the restrictions. Bring needed medicines, monitoring equipment and an appropriate snack for afterward, but wait until staff confirm it is safe to eat.

sections.heading: Tell staff honestly if the plan was not followed
paragraphs: If you eat, drink or take something outside the instructions, contact the service and explain what, how much and when. Do not hide it, cancel automatically or induce vomiting; staff decide whether to proceed or rearrange safely. If the appointment is delayed, ask for updated instructions instead of continuing an indefinite fast or drinking without checking. After the procedure, resume food, fluids and medicines according to the discharge plan. Some tests or treatments require further restrictions. Ask who to contact if you feel unwell or cannot keep fluids down.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a blood test without clear instructions
examples.text: Alina is told she needs blood tests but receives no fasting advice. She calls the service to ask which tests require fasting and whether water and her usual medicine are allowed. She does not skip breakfast simply because a friend did.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: milk before a procedure
examples.text: Dritan adds milk to a drink during his restricted period. He tells the department what he drank and when. The team decides what is safe; he does not conceal it to avoid a possible delay.

questions: Do I need to fast, and what are the exact food and drink instructions for this appointment?
What is the plan for each medicine and for diabetes or other conditions during fasting?
Who should I contact if I break the fast, the procedure is delayed or I become unwell?
